By analyzing the general properties of this system, we demonstrate that duality transformations, which convert one species into the other, effectively generate equivalent systems. Therefore, any physical aspect of the system represents a dual description for the same fundamental physics. Through this duality, systems with a highly doped region can be transformed into systems with a sparse distribution of the same species. Additionally, our holographic setup allows us to investigate the emergence of a gap in the sparse systems, which cannot be understood using the duality alone. In the process, we identify a phase transition between two states with a similar energy, yet one has a gap and the other does not. This gap can also be interpreted as a pseudogap, which arises from interactions between particles that are not paired. Furthermore, our study reveals that the s-wave pairing that develops in these systems over a low-temperature range is actually a result of unfolding the high-density sector of the same system. Consequently, the hole-doped state represents a dual description of the electron-doped state, which is reached through the inverse process of unfolding. As a result, attempts to study the electron-doped state using the hole-doped state as a reference will inevitably involve considering the effects of unfolding, which are more pronounced in systems with a higher degree of density due to the presence of flat bands. The emergence of the pseudogap and the properties of the two states that arise from folding and unfolding are therefore both general properties of flat bands that are brought about by high- and low-density matter coupled together.

Here, we introduce a formal framework to identify and quantify social bias present in data collections. Here are the key aspects of our approach:

  -   We define social bias as an unfair distribution of a given attribute across different categories, such as gender or racial disparities.
  -   To quantify this bias, we employ a metric called the "relative frequency ratio" (RFR), which calculates the average proportion of a specific attribute present in each category, relative to the overall distribution of that attribute across all categories.
  -   To determine statistical significance, we utilize a confidence interval framework, including both traditional and bootstrapping methods.
  -   We demonstrate the application of our approach through a series of experiments conducted on diverse datasets spanning text, images, and audio.

Additionally, it offers features for comparing multiple datasets simultaneously, which can be reached at https://social-bias.fallen.org/comparison. have long been the cornerstone for sequence-based predictions, despite being largely unexplored in the context of categorical sequences. The standard RNN architecture loses significant information over long sequences due to its inherent vanishing gradient issue. In contrast, our novel Categorical RNN (CatRNN) model leverages a modulated gateway function to dynamically adjust the influence of prior states on current outputs, thereby enabling efficient processing of long sequences. Furthermore, we introduce an RNN cell called CatRNN-TC (Tensor-Convolusion) cell that addresses both the vanishing gradient issue and insufficient local information by integrating a convolutional component to filter and reset the cell state. The CatRNN-TC cell was successfully applied to two challenging prediction tasks involving short and lengthy categorical sequences, outperforming our baseline RNN models in terms of accuracy. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ghrua/CatRNN. In this study, we introduce a novel approach based on robust optimization to address this issue. We first define a metric for transmission line flexibility and then establish a robust framework to determine minimum security margins under uncertain load conditions. To solve this problem efficiently, we derive a computationally simpler alternative formulation and apply it to a real-world power system. Our results show that our method can process large-scale systems quickly and provides insight into the distribution of security margins across transmission lines. Our study provides a robust foundation for reevaluating transmission line security margins and flexibility in the planning of future power systems. Coupling a conventional s-wave superconductor to an isolated superconducting phase-jump defect creates a unique, unidirectional Josephson effect. As a consequence, a conventional sine-Gordon model is unable to accurately describe this phenomenon. Instead, a 1D model featuring disordered "kinks" within a superconducting phase-coherent state is able to capture the essential features of this effect. Within this framework, the density of states for a finite-size system is computationally determined at various velocities, yielding a comprehensive understanding of the spectrum. The results show that the discrete nature of kinks significantly impacts the density of states, inducing multiple gaps within the spectrum in contrast to the gap structure predicted by the sine-Gordon model. Moreover, the presence of backscattered kinks leads to an asymmetry in the density of states, a phenomenon that may be experimentally verified via measurement of the critical current or the persistence of a non-zero supercurrent at temperatures well below the superconducting gap. The predicted effects are anticipated to be most pronounced in systems where the size of the defect approaches the length of coherence in the superconductor, a scenario that includes both large and small type-I superconductors. We examine how to balance the trade-off between these two factors for two optimization problems: mean-average-conditional-variace and online linear optimization. Furthermore, our study introduces new regret bounds that are more comprehensive, incorporating both the margin caused by adversarial data and the rate at which new data arrives. number of software developers has exponentially increased in correlation with the growth of software-dependent industries.  Despite this rise, a significant number of developed software remain in a state of incompatibility with newly emerging technologies.  This phenomenon is addressed in this research as "technological obsolescence" and its prevalence is evidenced by the numerous challenges faced by modern developers in maintaining existing software.  A key contributor to this issue is the continuous evolution of programming languages, which often results in a significant shift in language syntax and functionality over time.  This issue achieves a critical momentum with the release of each new operating system, as it forces developers to reevaluate their existing software compatibility.  This research introduces a novel approach to addressing this issue by defining a set of core capabilities for each programming language, which remains unaffected by changes in the operating system or other external factors.  A demonstration of this approach is presented through the creation of a security subsystem using the C++ language, which was successfully integrated into the Windows OS.  This research also provides the opportunity for future exploration of its theoretical aspects.  Ultimately, this approach has the potential to revolutionize the way we view the concept of technological obsolescence and software development as a whole.

Various optimal control approaches have been proposed to contend with the uncertain aspects of the disease's model, especially in cases where the model's parameters are subject to random fluctuations. In this study, we explore a different strategy, one that views the unpredictable aspects of the model as a structured disturbance. We then apply differential algebra to derive a parametric optimal control problem whose solutions yield a set of equations that can be employed to determine effective control measures for multiple types of pandemics, including flu and SARS-CoV-2, without randomized components. Our methodology enables policymakers to determine a one-size-fits-all set of policies that can be applied across various epidemic scenarios, thus shortening the time it takes to respond to an outbreak. Through the use of simulated data, we demonstrate how our approach can be applied to guide pandemic management at both national and international levels, as well as the benefits of its increased precision over other control methods. Finally, we highlight the practical implications of our findings for the pressing issue of how to manage outbreaks in regions where there are ongoing transmission chains. This research is an outcome of the author's involvement in the NSF's COVID-19 Redux Project, a collaborative effort among researchers from mathematics, computer science, biology, medicine, epidemiology, policy, and journalism to increase public understanding of the complexities of pandemic management through various media.

  These notes introduce the key concepts in the recent proofs of the minimal surface conjecture and the Penrose inequality due to Nelson and Souzaeldi, as well as the related work of Sharp.

  Specifically, the notes cover Almgren's minimal plateaus, the blow-up analysis for the mean-curvature flow, the Ricci flow and its relation to the Yamabe flow, harmonic functions and the Jacobian, and Sobolev inequality on manifolds. 

  The notes also outline the approaches to establishing sharp bounds on the first non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian on spheres and hyperbolic planes. 

  Finally, the notes conclude with the application of these results to the proof of the minimal surface conjecture and the Penrose inequality.

This limitation is addressed in our proposed MultiAmbigUNMT system, which leverages a novel combination of techniques to encode the complex meanings behind words, syllables, characters, and phrases. Based on the monolithic encoder model Universal Neural Machine Translation, our system incorporates multiple parallel encoders to process distinct levels of linguistic elements. Each encoder is pre-trained with a range of tasks including WordPiece prediction, character-level language modeling, and syntactic tree reconstruction. Ultimately, our experimental results indicate that our multi-encoder framework achieves the best performance overall, outperforming both single encoder universal models and carefully tuned pipeline systems. Moreover, the model's capability to decode ambiguites behind words, syllables, characters, and phrases is consistently reflected in its translation metrics scores. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/leda3t/MAUNMT. 

  Although successful in NMT, the MultiAmbigUNMT system's feasibility for other neural code models remains a topic for further research. Additionally, the lack of fully parallel corpora poses significant challenges for the model's applicability to low-resource and cross-language scenarios. To address the former issue, we explore alternative techniques for encoding diverse linguistic elements, such as multi-head attention and sum-based encoder combinations. Meanwhile, the model's applicability to low-resource and cross-language scenarios is investigated in the companion paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13744. Firstly, we propose a metric between sets of probability measures that is based on the worst-case transport cost between any two measures within those sets and maintains key OT properties, including symmetry and non-increasingness with respect to set inclusion. We then establish the convergence of empirical estimators of this set metric, providing a robust way to solve the multiple-source OT problem. Two common methods, the wavelet denoising technique and the Bayesian approach, have gained significant attention in recent years.  This paper delves into these filtering methods, presenting their underlying principles, applications, and future directions. Finally, we highlight the potential of this approach by suggesting possible variations and extensions, along with reasons why they are worth exploring in the field of EEG signal processing. This work has the potential to enhance the accuracy of EEG signal processing, providing implications for the diagnosis of neurological disorders and the development of brain-computer interfaces. Despite the robust performance of these large models in various tasks, a notable shortcoming exists in their robustness against unforeseen situations.  For instance, a model trained to generate coherent paragraphs may struggle when presented with bizarre input contents.  Our research centers around developing flexible models capable of producing meaningful text given any input, irrespective of its content.  A key challenge in achieving this goal exists in creating a suitable dataset. By comparing observed and simulated galaxy profiles, previous studies have validated this approach. However, these studies have primarily considered bright galaxies within a limited radial range and often relied on average profiles rather than individual galaxy comparisons. This research reexamines the relationship between galaxy light and halo mass within a more comprehensive radial range, accounting for a broader range of galaxy magnitudes. Instead, this study discovers a continuous distribution of galaxies within their halos, varying significantly depending on the magnitude of the galaxy. It begins with a comprehensive radial profile that accounts for all galaxies within a specific range of magnitudes, then divides this profile into distinct sections based on their distance from the halo center. By comparing these sections and varying the minimum magnitude considered, this approach allows for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between galaxy light and halo mass. By doing so, it effectively breaks down the four-scale model into multiple profiles for different galaxy magnitudes, confirming that the distinction between these categories depends heavily on these magnitudes. This study also shows that the good agreement between observed and simulated galaxy profiles within a limited radial range may hide significant discrepancies when considering a broader range of galaxy magnitudes, thereby underscoring the necessity of incorporating such magnitudes when modeling this relationship. This study focuses on the comprehension of repetitive patterns found in the syntax of coordinated clauses, specifically examining how readers anticipate and interpret the structure of embedded clauses within a complex syntactic framework. A recently devised method to analyze the comprehension of natural language using artificial neural networks is used to assess readers' expectations of the syntax of embedded clauses following coordination. A novel finding indicates that readers primarily focus on the level of branching in the embedded clause's syntax and not the entire complex sentence structure. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the comprehension of sentence meanings depends on the combination of meanings from the coordinated clauses rather than the overall syntax of the sentence. It has been hypothesized that the generation of natural language with repetitive patterns involves a hierarchical combination of smaller syntactic fragments, and results from a related experiment support this hypothesis. In contrast, the comprehension of such patterns appears to be driven by a more localized processing of syntactic elements. A possible explanation for this discrepancy is presented, emphasizing the distinct challenges involved in comprehending and generating natural language with repetitive patterns. In addition, potential implications and avenues for further research in this area are discussed.

However, the effectiveness of such antennas in wireless sensing and tracking depends on the signal intensity and its variation with the target's location.  To optimize spatial sensitivity, we propose a novel idea of leveraging quasi-optical properties through intensity maximization techniques, taking into account multipath effects that influence signal strength at different points.  To tackle this complex problem, we draw on physics-based models, incorporating ray tracing and general electromagnetic theory, and derive a objective function that prioritizes intensity over accuracy in delay estimates.  To resolve the resulting nonlinear optimization challenge, we explore various methods - including Lagrange multipliers, simulated annealing, and reinforcement learning - to identify a suitable approach for our scenario and offer guidance on tuning algorithm parameters.  Through numerical experiments and real-world implementations, we evaluate and compare the performance of our proposed solutions.  The resulting code is now openly accessible, enabling other researchers to build upon our work and adapt our methods to their unique antenna configurations.  To further extend our research, we invite collaborators to join a related project, which is openly hosted on a collaborative platform.  Ultimately, our innovative approach has the potential to enhance wireless sensing and tracking technology, particularly in settings where physical access is limited or complex - such as in overhaul maintenance, where attaching targets to surfaces may not be feasible, or in locations with distinct indoor-outdoor transitions.  To take this a step further, we explore a related project that focuses on optimizing antenna design itself, rather than the approach presented here, which centers around adapting existing designs to improve wireless sensing and tracking.  This complementary project is also openly accessible and could serve as a starting point for designing purpose-built antennas from scratch. neural networks has been a challenge, especially when it comes to characterizing their ability to approximate complex functions across all possible input domains. This concept is crucial in understanding two important issues related to neural networks: their ability to achieve perfect performance on training data (a phenomenon known as "vacuous optimality"); and the extent to which neural networks can be trusted to perform well in real-world situations after being trained on easily manipulable datasets. To investigate these issues, we propose a new metric called "domain complexity," which measures the extent to which a function computed by a neural network deviates from the simplest possible case, taking into account all possible input data. To illustrate the practical value of this metric, we investigated its application to several real-world datasets, discovering that the complexity of the computed functions varies significantly depending on the dataset, and that the relationship between the accuracy of the predictions and the complexity of the computed functions is not always straightforward. Lastly, we explored various methods for reducing the complexity of the computed functions while maintaining the same level of prediction accuracy, and found that certain techniques were more effective than others in certain situations. Overall, our research highlights the importance of carefully examining the behavior of neural networks in both theoretical and practical contexts.

This study examines how various time series analysis techniques treat the natural variability of a system in proportion to its mean response, applying them to the linear Stefan problem. We evaluated ten common methods: Linear Regression, Pre-Whitening, Cross-Correlation, Optimal Linear Estimation, Filling in Missing Data, Scaling, Shift Correction, Detrended Analysis, Trend Removal, and None. We calculated the relative importance of natural variability in relation to the system's response for each method, quantifying this relationship as a coefficient. Our results show that most time series analysis techniques overestimate a system's response due to an insufficient account of natural variability, with the exception of Optimal Linear Estimation. Notably, the choice of analysis technique can result in a 300-fold difference in the apparent sensitivity of a system. This finding highlights the potential misinterpretation of system response when the contribution of natural variability is not adequately considered. It is therefore crucial to choose a time series analysis technique that accurately accounts for this contribution, taking into account the system's specific characteristics, to avoid misleading conclusions in scientific studies. The HESS system went into operation in 2003 and has successfully identified numerous particle accelerators in the VHF range within the Milky Way and beyond.  As the most sensitive ground-based detector for the VHF range, HESS has significantly contributed to the understanding of these accelerators and their particle spectra.  In 2019, the HESS sensitivity to the VHF range was enhanced with the addition of five new telescopes in the same location, significantly improving its sensitivity and reach. To estimate the minimum detectable energy of HESS, a statistical approach that takes into account the angle of the particle accelerator and the energy of the detected particles is employed, effectively modeling the detection process as a stochastic process. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A key distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. This work provides a significant step towards developing more complex models that can account for single-phase Darcy flow within a more nuanced description of fractures, such as those found in nature, which often have varying levels of permeability. This will be an area we continue to explore in our upcoming research on modeling two-phase flow within a more broadly defined fracture space. The degree of coordination achieved in these scenarios is captured by a new metric called the coordination persistence factor, which accounts for the stability of coordination over time. The results of our research have implications for the development of decentralized velocity control algorithms, as well as potential applications in fields like animal swarm optimization. Despite its high sensitivity, LISA measurements will be influenced by the fluctuations of the satellite's position relative to a fixed observer on Earth, which poses a significant challenge for parameter estimation, often referred to as the light travel time effect. To offer the most accurate predictions possible for the observations it will make, LISA needs to take into account not just its own instrumental errors but also the impact of its elliptical orbit around the Sun, which causes variations in the distance between the satellite and the Earth over the course of its 1.5-year cycle. In this research, we examine how the LISA detector's oscillating movements affect the accuracy of its measurements of the masses of compact binary black hole systems as they merge. We analyze three distinct configurations for LISA's pairwise detections, evaluating how they are impacted by the fluctuations of the satellite's position relative to a fixed observer on Earth and the variations in the distance between the satellite and the Earth over the course of its 1.5-year cycle. We discovered that the most coherent pair of detections results in the most significant instrumental error, with a minimal impact of the light travel time effect when considering all possible coherent pairs of detections. To address this issue, we investigated possible solutions such as assigning different weights to the two detectors of the LISA trio and establishing a fixed reference frame for the measurements made by the satellite, either individually or collectively. We found that assigning different weights to the two detectors of the LISA trio leads to an improvement of up to a factor of 5 in the accuracy of the mass measurements when considering all possible coherent pairs of detections. Furthermore, we discovered that establishing a fixed reference frame for the measurements made by the satellite, either individually or collectively, results in an improvement of up to a factor of 128 in the accuracy of the mass measurements when considering all possible coherent pairs of detections. Lastly, we analyzed a variety of LISA mission scenarios and forecasted the impact of the light travel time effect on the measurement of binary black hole merger parameters, predicting a maximum improvement of up to a factor of 102 in the accuracy of mass measurements with the final configuration of the LISA trio. Ultimately, this research highlights the significance of taking the light travel time effect into account when simulating the observations LISA will make of compact binary black hole mergers. In these competitions, pairings of experienced players participate, often drawing from the largest cohort of all - the ATP doubles rankings.  Unlike singles, where the outcome depends on a single player's performance, doubles rely on the collaboration of two highly skilled athletes. As a buffer against such exploits, researchers have already discovered over a thousand potential attack vectors.  In response to these findings, various software developers are reviewing their codebases, identifying areas that require patching.  As a preliminary step to a formal vulnerability assessment, we conducted an informal analysis of 100 popular Java projects on Maven Central, assessing their susceptibility to log4j exploitation.  Our evaluation criteria focused on whether a project can run malicious URLs or send unsolicited data over the network when log4j is compromised.  Based on our tests, we found that approximately 31% of these projects are vulnerable to this type of exploitation.  Strikingly, we observed that even though many developers have already fixed their codebases, we discovered numerous projects with no response indicating further action is needed.  In this study, we encourage developers to review their dependencies regularly and explore a variety of techniques for detecting potentially malicious behavior in Java applications.  As an example of an analysis tool, we introduce Retsup, a runtime evaluation system designed to identify areas of uncertainty within Java code.  Retsup's capabilities can contribute to enhanced security of software systems, not only in relation to log4j but also in the context of other trust infrastructures.  As part of our contribution to mitigating the effects of log4j, we are making the Retsup framework publicly available to support the ongoing efforts of the Java development community.  Through a series of use cases and technical specifications, we are providing a blueprint for other researchers to build on this concept and explore related areas of uncertain code within Java applications.  Future Work: Future research will focus on overcoming limitations, validating
empirically the theoretical findings, and exploring new areas of study (e.g., multi-
stakeholder ecosystems). 
 

 Citation: Younès, M. M., & Lakhani, M. Formalizing Technological Ecosystems and
their Optimal Configuration. Journal of the Association for Information Science
and Technology. DOI: 10.1002/asi.22427. 
 

 Abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to analyzing technological
ecosystems as interconnected networks of interdependent components, followed by a
detailed examination of a specific ecosystem consisting of developers, applications,
and users, ultimately leading to the development of an algorithm for identifying
the optimal configuration of this ecosystem based on specific goals. 
 

 Keywords: Technological Ecosystems, Software Ecosystems, Platform Optimization

This study adapts the technique of correcting for detector inefficiency in the context of homodyne detection to obtain an accurate representation of squeezed states within a noisy detector system. Results show that even with inefficient detection, a homodyne measurement can still demonstrate optimal performance in distinguishing squeezed states from their classical counterparts.  The findings also indicate that in order to achieve maximum success in this task, the detection system should strive for balanced efficiency, one that is neither too sensitive nor too insensitve.  In practical terms, this can be interpreted as the need for a middle-ground gain in efficiency when comparing the two-dimensional detection system to a more nuanced model that takes into account various levels of inefficiency within the detector.  When evaluating the performance of a homodyne detector that is inefficient due to various loss mechanisms, such as photon loss and electrical loss, the results indicate that the optimal success probability in identifying squeezed states from their classical counterparts undergoes a more substantial degradation.  In contrast, a combination of homodyne detection and another measurement method, such as the one used in anti-squeezed states, can still demonstrate optimal performance even when the detection system is inefficient.  Finally, the study proposes the use of a more complex model for simulating homodyne detection in matrix-form representation, such as in systems based on the Heisenberg model, with a straightforward adaptation of the squeezing operation within this context.  This work provides a foundation for investigating the impact of detector inefficiency on other continuous-variable quantum states and applications. Observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and MMT enable us to gather information about the redshifted, light curve of the GRB's early phase, which we model to understand its variability.  Analyzing this variability, we identify a feature in the spectrum that displays a 1 second period and is absent in the later stages of the GRB.  Despite initial speculation that this feature could be a gravitational wave emission caused by two compact objects, we find a conflicting outcome when we run the detectors simulation with two neutron stars or a neutron star and black hole, which do not produce the observed light curve.  However, if we incorporate the presence of a massive object and treat the neutron star as an inner observer who sees the electromagnetic emission of the black hole, we get a result that closely resembles the observed data, which suggests that the neutron star blocks the electromagnetic emission of the black hole during the 1 second period, and then falls into it, which results in the emission of gravitational waves in the later stages of the GRB.  We also identify the distance to this event as 5.42 Gpc, which if true would make GRB 130426A the most distant neutron star candidate detected so far, and estimate its energy at isotropic rest frame as (4.2+1.5/-1.2) x 10^51 erg/s, which if true would make it the most energetic neutron star detected so far. A key aspect of this theory is the concept of thin boundary layers, which can be modeled using asymptotic equations and analyzed using various techniques, including the use of scaling, transformation, and expansion methods. A key challenge in this process involves detecting hidden faults that occur within the feedback loop, making it essential to examine new detection methods. This study introduces a novel approach using differential flatness for fault detection in control loops affected by hidden faults. Firstly, we establish a differential flatness-based normal form for a general nonlinear system, transforming it into a parametrized system where the output equals a differentiable function of the parameters and their integrals. Secondly, we create a reference trajectory with a known fault within the output's differentiable function. Thirdly, we compare the actual system's output with the predicted output based on the reference trajectory, detecting any discrepancies as evidence of a hidden fault. A key distinction of this model is that it allows for the derivation of an exact, two-body solution, which is presented along with the derived parameters for this specific solution.  This new metric meets the requirements of having recharge cycles of minimal length, minimal energy consumption, and the ability to maintain stability for a prolonged period as demonstrated by an instability growth rate factor lower than 1.  With this model, the length of an interstellar journey to a nearby star like Proxima could be essentially instantaneous in its effective trajectory, despite being bounded by the speed of light in real time.  Furthermore, this model allows for the creation of stable warps with optimal characteristics for trips to the Moon, Mars, and other shorter-distance missions.  A possible experimental design is also presented to give a realistic figure for creating such stable warps, which could be as small as 10 meters in diameter, requiring an energy amount comparable to that of today's largest particle colliders.  This model gives hope that a viable, real-world application of the Alcubierre warp drive concept could be developed, potentially revolutionizing space travel in the near future.  The proposed model is called the Pre-Post-Feynman Alcubierre Warp Drive Model, which can be shortened to PPFAWDM for simplicity.   analysis to examine the underlying structure of a music understanding system.
  By zooming in on a system's components, we assess its ability to identify
  key features of a concept and its accompanying melody, as well as its
  capacity to pinpoint essential themes within a broader musical passage.
  Our "search" method allows us to evaluate the system's performance on abstract
  concepts and musical theories, such as chord progressions, in much the same
  way that we assess its ability to understand specific melodies.  We show

  interpretations.  Ultimately, our approach provides a method for systematically

  composition.  We have applied this approach to develop a more effective

These findings build on the foundation established by the Quantum Reverse Schur algorithm, which was first introduced in 2016. The underlying model considered here is a multi-particle system comprised of scalar particles, and all proofs are based on the unitarity of the quantum scattering operator for a specific type of scattering interaction. managers valuable information on how to structure the placement system to achieve 
the best results for various TANF recipient groups. The method employed in this 
chapter can be adapted to examine the effects of other program interventions. lead halide perovskite material has
been attributed to various factors, with a proposed association to its inherent
defect structure.  Through a combination of experimental measurements and
theoretical simulations, we have identified a perceived "defect" as actually an
integral component of the material's crystal, thereby hindering both
electron and hole mobility.  By accurately modeling this defect structure,
we have been able to replicate the measured charge carrier lifetimes and
mobilities, as well as optic/electric properties, all without the need for
additional adjustments.  We have also demonstrated that this defect can be
reduced in size through temperature changes and by adding certain dopants,
thereby potentially leading to improvements in perovskite photovoltaic device
performance.  Furthermore, our research reveals that efforts to minimize this
defect may instead accelerate the recombination of charge carriers, a previously
unanticipated finding that must be considered when developing perovskite
technologies.  Ultimately, this research positions us to accurately investigate
the perovskite material's property variations and potential performance limitations
at different levels of detail, allowing us to effectively assess the impact of
any changes on the material's charge carrier behavior.  Through this work, we have
identified a perovskiteite defect as a significant obstacle to achieving high
device performance, and have developed a framework for analyzing and addressing
this issue, which will be vital as research moves towards a Vaughan-Prange defect
structure in perovskite materials.  This defect structure is anticipated to be
achieved as the material's vaughanite-to-perovskiteite transformation is reversed,
with the V$^{2+}$ ions again becoming loosely bound to the perovskiteite sites,
but this time without the occurrence of the $V_{V}a$ defect, thus yielding a

mark a significant departure from the traditional perovskite material, with the

analogous to an silicon vacancy, with the possible emergence of a perovskiteite

However, identifying the most informative samples is computationally expensive due to the need to recalculate training losses for various data subsets.  A previously proposed method, Deep Information Flow (DIF), addressed this challenge by developing an algorithm to efficiently determine the most informative samples by approximating the expected training loss for each data point. Experiments demonstrating the efficacy and efficiency of DAS across multiple tasks, particularly in the context of self-supervised and label-efficient learning, highlight its superiority over existing adaptive sampling methods. This approach often assumes that turbulence influences the light wave front's behavior in a manner equivalent to a random phase shift, without fully accounting for the consequences of turbulence on the radius of the meteor's tail. In fact, turbulence can cause the tail to enlarge, affecting the measurement process and resulting in inaccurately estimated meteor paths if this effect is neglected. This study presents a new method for modeling the effects of atmospheric turbulence to improve the accuracy of optical meteor trajectory calculations. The model is based on an improved algorithm that takes into consideration the unique characteristics of the meteoroid's shape and its movement, as well as the inherent randomness of turbulence. By numerically analyzing this model under various conditions, we demonstrate that our new approach significantly reduces errors in trajectory estimations, even with limited observational data. Furthermore, the model is integrated into a comprehensive meteoroid trajectory simulation, allowing for more precise predictions of the conditions experienced by the meteoroid as it enters the Earth's atmosphere. The results of this implementation are validated through comparisons with actual meteor events, yielding a high degree of accuracy in predictions of meteoroid path, temperature, and atmospheric conditions. The new model's higher precision is achieved despite the limitations of range-finding data, which are inherently incomplete due to the ephemeral nature of optical meteor events. To facilitate further research and the sharing of meteoroid data, the improved model is made available as an open-source contribution. The study also explores various metrics for assessing the quality of meteoroid predictions, which can be minimal, typically consisting of radar observations of a meteoroid over a few seconds. In such cases, the model is validated to provide accurate predictions of the meteoroid's trajectory, temperature, and atmospheric conditions, as shown through comparisons with actual meteor events. The results of these comparisons indicate a high degree of accuracy in predictions of meteoroid path, radius, and pressure, even with the limited amount of data available from these events. The study also explores various metrics for assessing the quality of meteoroid predictions, which can be used to prioritize the processing of data for high-priority targets, such as near-Earth asteroids. The emergence of embedded systems that can process visual data efficiently has also been observed in recent times.  In the context of object detection, accurate matching of the model's output to the image's actual contents is paramount.  Nonetheless, research on the topic of accuracy versus resource consumption for object detection on embedded systems has been limited to examining how various algorithms and models affect the balance of the two factors on specific devices.  Our research offers a novel approach by investigating how different algorithm types and model architectures impact the balance of accuracy and resource consumption across multiple embedded systems.  In practice, our method enables the selection of the most accurate model that can run within a predetermined resource constraint on a particular device, thus increasing the potential for data efficiency enhancements.  We applied this approach to examining the balance of accuracy and resource consumption across eight diverse embedded systems utilizing the popular MS COCO dataset, and also explored alternative datasets for comprehensive comparison.  In conclusion, our research provides a comprehensive overview of the object detection field on embedded systems, and the associated data sets, while highlighting the complex interaction between accuracy and resource consumption. Formally, the Koopman operator is defined as a set of state transformation functions that, when applied to any given state, result in the future state at a specified time interval. This paper delves into the derivation of the Koopman operator and its invariant measure, known as the state transformation function and probability measure, within the context of discrete-time dynamic systems. The work presents two primary methodologies: the first involves constructing the Koopman operator through its transition matrices, while the second involves deriving the state transformation function directly from the system's equations of motion. The paper also explores specific system types, including stochastic systems, multi-body systems, and their applications to the dynamics of planetary systems and genetic networks. The described methodologies provide a theoretical foundation for the analysis of complex dynamic systems and can be extended to continuous-time systems. We compared the predictive performance of multiple algorithms, including single decision trees, bagged decision trees, and variants of the random forest algorithm. Our primary innovation involves applying bagging not only to individual decision trees but also to the ensemble models obtained through further bagging. We achieved the latter by repeatedly constructing random forest models and combining their predictions. Our results indicate that this method outperforms traditional bagging techniques while offering computational efficiency advantages. We propose that selecting the number of trees in each random forest model should be a subject of optimization rather than a fixed parameter. Through a range of experiments, we demonstrated the superiority of this approach over both single decision trees and traditional bagging methods. Our research reveals that many popular global model-agnostic feature importance methods yield results that are highly influenced by the features themselves, rather than providing a unbiased evaluation of feature importance as claimed.  In order to validate this finding, a comprehensive set of evaluation methods was devised and applied to a diverse range of datasets featuring both synthetic and real-world data.  The results show that many of these methods consistently rank features according to their dependence on the target variable, rather than providing a unbiased evaluation of feature importance as claimed.  In the process of evaluating these methods a phenomenon was observed - the way effects are scaled or normalized has a significant impact on the ranking of features.  In addition, many of these methods were found to be highly sensitive to changes in dataset scale, demonstrating that feature importance assessments are not stable over changes in dataset normalization.  In the end, our research implies that selection of a single best global model-agnostic feature importance method is not possible, rather it depends on the specific characteristics of the dataset in question.  In order to address this, a framework for evaluation and comparison of multiple methods was proposed, providing a set of easy to use tools for assessment and comparison of different methods across different datasets. Our findings show that in a three-valley model, an infinite dark soliton train can only be achieved if the average electron energy is greater than a specific threshold, a result confirmed by our experimental observations. An energy below this threshold results in unstable, short-lived dark soliton trains. Conversely, average electron energies exceeding a certain other threshold lead to wave function destruction and the emergence of stable, two-hump solitons in a GaAs system, albeit not observed in our experiments. The theoretical proposal of a three-valley model for GaP allows for the exploration of infinite, stable dark soliton trains in this material.  Furthermore, our experimental and theoretical analyses demonstrate that in a three-valley model, the minimum energy required to maintain an infinite dark soliton train in GaP is significantly higher when compared to GaAs.  Additionally, our experiments demonstrate the successful creation of GaP dark solitons via a pair of phase-displaced GaAs dark solitons, a phenomenon not fully understood and in need of further theoretical investigation.  The formation of these GaP dark solitons is accompanied by a significant increase in energy within the valley at which the soliton is formed, as well as a corresponding decrease in energy within the opposing valley, a phenomenon not observed when creating GaAs dark solitons.  A theoretical two-bands model is also presented to better comprehend the creation of GaAs dark solitons, a model that fails to capture the multivalley behavior of electrons in this material. We then establish that any possible configuration of the body can be represented by a four-dimensional parametric equation, and its velocity is determined by a linear combination of the same fixed basis vectors. We proceed to derive a key mathematical formula, often referred to as the rotation velocity formula, which enables us to calculate the rate of change of any coordinate with respect to time. We then apply this formula to obtain two important results: one relating the rotation velocity to the angular velocity of the body, and the other expressing the rotation velocity in terms of the body's velocity and direction within space. We proceed to explore how to apply these results to solve problems involving rigid bodies moving within space, by first identifying key reference frames, determining the body's velocity and direction within these frames, and finally using the rotation velocity formula to calculate its angular velocity. We then present a series of example problems to demonstrate how to use these techniques to solve real-world problems involving rigid bodies moving within space. We also introduce an alternative approach to solving these problems, one that involves expressing the body's velocity and angular velocity in terms of linear and angular velocities of key reference frames, and then combining these velocities to obtain the total velocity and angular velocity of the body. We then develop a more sophisticated model that takes into account the body's movement relative to these key reference frames, and demonstrate how to use this model to solve problems involving rigid bodies moving within space. The results of these experiments reveal significant improvements in computational times and overall system efficiency. Furthermore, the adaptable nature of this architecture has the potential to address more complex multi-tasking EFB requirements on UAVs, which can be owned by individual operators rather than large corporations. As such, this research is poised to play a part in promoting the safe and reliable adoption of UAVs in delivery services, which is a critical step towards these vehicles becoming an integrated part of civil aviation.

This study proposes a novel, range-based attention mechanism in a baseline universal correspondence network framework, capable of generating dense, pixel-to-pixel correspondences between images of different classes and then utilizing these correspondences to transfer annotations. We then establish that the 4-fold Abel-Jacobi map is surjective, which was previously shown by Diem under the assumption that the discriminant of $E$ is not a square.  We achieve our result by first identifying a specific quadratic field and a non-square discriminant quadratic field, both of which share a common prime factor of 37.  We then construct two supersingular elliptic curves over the algebraic closure of these fields.  We then demonstrate the existence of a 3-3-4 cycle among the K3 surfaces associated with these curves, which in turn enables us to construct our common torsion point.  We also propose another method to construct a common point using the Artin-Scheier theory.  We further demonstrate that Diem's result is the best possible by constructing a family of curves $y^2 = x^3 + d$, where $d$ varies among the integers from 1 to 5.  We claim that for each of these values of $d$, there is no share of a 4-fold Abel-Jacobi map among the curves in this family, except possibly when $d$ equals 0, which however is not covered by our theorem, as the curve in this case is the Fermat curve.  We also propose another method to construct this common point, which is based on the Gruenwald-Wang method, which however is known to be weaker than Diem's result, as it implies the existence of a 2-fold Abel-Jacobi map among the curves in this family, which is not the case when $d$ equals 1.  This method enables us to propose a conjecture about the existence of a share of an n-fold Abel-Jacobi map among the curves in this family for any $n$, which however is not the case when $n$ is greater than or equal to 3, as recently demonstrated by Kudla and Milller. distinguish between different water quality classes. Additionally, our analysis 
revealed that using all five parameters resulted in the best classification 
performance of 92.5% which was a significant improvement compared to using only 
two parameters and achieved a moderate accuracy of 65%. These findings have 
important implications for the selection of machine learning algorithms and 
water quality parameters in automated classification systems. Overall, our method 
offers a promising approach for the development of these systems and can be 
useful in preventing pollution hotspots and notifying authorities of 
abnormalities in water quality in real-time.  Water quality can be classified

good water quality whereas high turbidity is a sign of poor water quality.

pH level is an indicator of very poor water quality. Ultimately, the goal of 
this research is to design an automated water quality monitoring system that 
can immediately identify the class of water quality based on sensor data.

algorithms and understanding which ones work best in different situations.

monodromy around a singular point in the complex plane. This phenomenon was 
discovered by Stokes in 1877 and initially studied in relation to the equation $y^2-1=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(x-a_j^2)$ by Wilkinson in 1976. The objective of this study is to examine the six-order differential equation $y^6-\prod_{j=1}^{6}(x-b_j^2)=0$ to understand how the complex plane is divided in relation to the singular points and to identify the direction of monodromy around these points. It has been discovered that there are 42 possible arrangements of the singular points, but only 11 of these arrangements result in a Stokes line that extends infinitely in the complex plane. Additionally, it is observed that the direction of monodromy around a singular point can change direction in relation to that point, indicating that some points cause a change in direction at a singular point, while others do not, and that there is no pattern or correlation between the arrangement of the singular points and the change in direction of monodromy. It is also discovered that a change in direction of monodromy around a singular point is equivalent to a change in the direction of the imaginary part of the argument function $w(z)$ as it encircles the singular point. It is proposed that the points where the direction of monodromy changes could be referred to as Stokes points, and that the line where the direction of monodromy changes in the complex plane could be referred to as a Stokes line. It is also hypothesized that the change in direction of monodromy around a singular point is a necessary condition for the appearance of a Borel sum failure line in the complex plane. Studying near-sun asteroids allows for observations on how a tiny world maintains stability in the face of increasing solar radiation pressure and gravitational effects from its close proximity to the sun. Additionally, such asteroids exhibit diverse orbital paths, offering a framework for understanding dynamic phenomena such as comet tails and dust trails. Our conditional saddlepoint approximation leads to a more efficient computation compared to the standard method, which we demonstrate on two types of models: the slice mixture model and the Pitman-Yule beta process. completely different set of anonymous data. From a theoretical perspective,
this is a problem of using one dataset that contains sensitive information to
make predictions on another, unrelated dataset. In this research, we explore the
possibility of achieving this using Deep Neural Networks by analyzing the type
of data that can be accurately predicted, the type of data that can be used
for training, and the limitations of these predictions. Our results show that,
dependent on how the data is prepared and trained, it is possible to accurately
predict both training and test data, but this is largely an achievement of
overfitting rather than a genuine prediction. In reality, predicting data that
is either significantly larger or smaller than the training data is not possible
in reality. Furthermore, using a larger set of anonymous data that is related
to the target data does enhance predictions, but this comes at the cost of
increased data that may contain sensitive information. In conclusion, while Deep
Neural Networks do excel in predicting accurate outcomes on a completely different
set of anonymous data, this achievement is largely an extension of overfitting
rather than a genuine prediction.  Keywords: Deep Neural Networks, Predictive
Modeling, Sensitive Data, Anonymous Data, Overfitting.

Information Communication Technology (ICT) related misinformation, which poses a significant threat to public health and safety. This paper identifies a pressing need for an automated system able to identify and flag health-related misinformation spreading through ICT networks. To address this challenge, a hybrid system is proposed, combining artificial intelligence techniques with a network diffusion model to pinpoint and highlight false health information. The proposed system is tested on real-world data obtained from Twitter and yields promising results, outperforming existing methods and demonstrating an advanced ability to recognize health misinformation. Furthermore, our results reveal that health misinformation tends to converge to a smaller subset of sensitive topics, which can be identified and validated objectively. This insight holds practical value for healthcare professionals, clinicians, and researchers who need to track down such sensitive topics. The proposed system's source code is made publicly available for replication and replication instructions are provided. To investigate this, researchers have recently suggested a series of experiments that involve the study of $K$ and $D$ meson decays to address several fundamental questions regarding the Standard Model and its anomalies.  In this research, we propose introducing a fourth generation of heavy quarks with varying mass ratios, such as $m_t/m_b \approx 200$, which would significantly impact multiple physical processes.  The proposed theory predicts the presence of enhanced resonance peaks in $B$ and $K$ meson decays resulting from $b$ and $c$ heavy quarks for at least two scenarios: when the new scale of symmetry breaking is either much higher than the electroweak scale or comparable to it.  To verify this theory, we consider the contribution of a fifth dimension and a related "dilaton" particle that could be identified in meson decay events by analyzing the distribution of energy and angle data.  The proposed theory also predicts the solution to the $U_{\text{CS}}$ problem and provides a mechanism for generating the mass of light quarks via a form factor, which could lead to additional resonance peaks in meson decays.  To estimate these resonance peaks, we study the impact of a complex "dilaton" particle on $K$ and $D$ meson decays, particularly in processes such as $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ \nu($X$)$ and $D^+ \to K^0_S \ell^+ \ell'$, and predict the enhancement of these processes by one to three orders of magnitude, which could be confirmed by future experiments with high precision, ultimately confirming or refuting the proposed theory for the mass of light quarks. In this research, we examine the diffusion of information in online networks through opinion leading, where users explicitly convey their thoughts via posting updates. We refer to this process as "expressed influence" and investigate its mechanisms within real-world datasets obtained from Twitter and Baidu Tieba. By analyzing user interaction data, we identify two distinct types of expressed influence: direct diffusion, where the poster's followers engage with the shared content, and indirect diffusion, where the account is merely mentioned. As a result, a significant portion of information undergoes direct diffusion, while also experiencing continued indirect attention. We further observe fluctuating patterns of influence as users adapt to previous posting behaviors from nearby users. Ultimately, our study sheds light on the complex dynamics of online influence dissemination and provides insights into designing more effective information dissemination strategies within these networks. In so doing, we introduce a suite of open-source tools to facilitate further research in this area. deformation.  In order to address this shortcoming, a new approach is proposed,

By expressing the system's dynamics in terms of a set of first-order differential equations, we can determine if achieving precise control is possible, provided that there is some flexibility in the system's parameters. Specifically, if the system's open-loop transfer function has its zeros at zero or negative values, it is possible to design a controller that ensures the system's response converges to a stable equilibrium within a certain time frame. This framework is applied to two examples: controlling a second-order system with a zero at zero, and controlling a first-order system with a slow response. These examples illustrate how the system's response and settling time are affected by its natural frequency and damping ratio. Ultimately, this approach provides a clear, concise criterion for evaluating a system's controllability based on its open-loop transfer function. By considering both stability and settling time, this method facilitates controller design that takes into account the system's dynamic characteristics. This approach is particularly useful for manual controller design, but further research is needed to fully automate the design process. Although this method is primarily focused on linear time-invariant systems, it is also applicable to systems with nonlinear components, provided that the system can be reasonably approximated by a linear model over the desired operating range. In addition, this approach is relevant to various fields, including electrical engineering, mechanical engineering, aerospace engineering, and chemical engineering. Finally, this approach is not limited to any specific control structure, but rather is a fundamental requirement for both classical and modern control design methods, such as PID, lead-lag compensation, state-space placement, and optimal control. Our findings confirm that the threshold for primordial black hole formation can be higher than predicted by the 1-σ density fluctuation criterion, and the exact increase varies depending on the relation between density fluctuation scale and black hole mass. The ratio of primordial black hole mass to total mass density threshold can be either higher or lower than 10% and decreases towards shorter wavelength perturbations, ultimately resulting in no primordial black hole formation above a certain cutoff. The crossover in this behavior occurs when the fluctuation scale approaches about 100 times the primordial black hole radius. Our analysis also reveals that the primordial black hole formation process can be accurately modeled using the Press-Schechter formalism, and the agreement between this approach and our direct numerical simulations holds for density fluctuations with a relative variance below 0.01. For more massive primordial black holes, the formation process becomes less efficient, and the density of the universe plays a more significant role, but it has a minimal impact on the 10 Earth mass primordial black hole formation. Our study provides new insights into the limitations of Press-Schechter theory and the potential biases introduced by assuming all primordial black holes form from 1-σ density fluctuations, especially when considering the effects of perturbations with different wavelengths on black hole formation. These findings can be applied to both cosmological and laboratory settings, and the primordial black hole formation model developed here can be used to study the effects of various density fluctuations on black hole formation, which can be modified to fit specific scenarios. The code for our direct numerical simulations of primordial black hole formation is available upon request. The scale of the overdensity in our simulations can be adjusted to model black holes formed from either cosmological or laboratory-generated fluctuations. The primary variation in our simulations is the non-dimensional distance from the center of the overdensity, which affects the collapse of nearby matter and resulting black hole mass, as shown in Figure 4. The code can be used to generate the primordial black hole mass-to-total mass density ratio plot in Figure 5, as well as the distribution of primordial black hole masses formed from a given density distribution, as shown in the inset of Figure 5. The code can be modified to model different types of density distributions and fluctuations of various scales, which can be used to generate different primordial black hole mass distributions

and material variability of polycrystalline titanium on the generation of microorganisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. Two categories of surface roughness were identified: low-energy surfaces characterized by high roughness and high-energy surfaces with low roughness. The distribution, size, and shape of pores also influenced adhesion. Adhesion was greatest on surfaces with intermediate energy levels and was reduced on both high-energy and low-energy surfaces. Factors such as stress direction, anisotropy, and slip band density influenced the size and distribution of pores. Some factors that contribute to adhesion, such as stress direction and slip band density, were not significantly affected by the material.  Overall, the study suggests that neither surface energy nor stress direction alone is sufficient to explain the distribution and size of pores, and thus the likelihood of bacterial adhesion. Instead, a combination of these factors is responsible. Variables that contribute to adhesion in titanium can be categorized into three groups: material variables (surface energy, stress), structure variables (pore size and distribution), and their combined effects (adhesion). Further research is needed to fully understand the variables that contribute to adhesion in titanium and how they interact with each other and other factors that contribute to infection. Ultimately, this knowledge can be used to develop more effective strategies for preventing infection in titanium components.

Abstract: 
This study examines the interaction between stress anisotropy and slip bands on bacterial adhesion in titanium.  It shows that neither stress anisotropy nor slip bands alone are sufficient to explain the distribution and size of pores, and thus the likelihood of bacterial adhesion.  Instead, a combination of these factors is responsible.  Variables that contribute to adhesion in titanium can be categorized into three groups: material variables (surface energy, stress), structure variables (pore size and distribution), and their combined effects (adhesion).  Further research is needed to fully understand the variables that contribute to adhesion in titanium and how they interact with each other and other factors that contribute to infection.  Ultimately, this knowledge can be used to develop more effective strategies for preventing infection in titanium components.

As an example, a laser pulse with an intensity of $10^{24}$ W/cm$^2$ and 1 ps duration can be produced with an electron beam carrying 1 nC in 1 ps.  This capability can be applied to the generation of ultra-high-intensity laser pulses in multiple directions.  As an extension of this concept, a chain of connected RF cavities can produce multi-directional, multi-petawatt laser pulses from a single electron beam, spanning an angle of approximately 2$\pi$.  This configuration can be used to enhance laser pulse generation in the context of the two-stage laser system proposed for space-based laser pulse generation, where a low-power laser pulse produced in Earth orbit is amplified in intensity by an electron beam-driven laser pulse in the photon star phenomenon, resulting in a much-intensified laser pulse that can be detected on the surface of Earth.   We propose an external weak formulation (EWF) of fractional boundary control problems, which involves transforming the problem from a boundary control setting to an external force one, while maintaining the same degrees of freedom. This strategy is employed to overcome non- uniqueness issues commonly found in such problems. A notable advantage of the EWF is its ability to be solved via low-order finite element methods, which provides a more manageable alternative to higher-order methods required for the original problem. We demonstrate the efficacy of the EWF by applying it to a variety of fractional boundary control problems, before validating the performance of the new strategy through numerous numerical experiments.

The main challenge to certifying such networks lies in the high computational costs associated with central differences, making tensor train decomposition a viable solution to this problem. By leveraging a finite difference approximation that demands significantly fewer computations per layer, CertNN-TT demonstrates the potential to certify non-sparse, ReLU-based neural networks by breaking down the derivation of certifiable robustness into individual network layers. The performance of CertNN-TT is showcased through a series of experiments involving the certification of both handwritten and natural image classifiers. The results indicate that CertNN-TT is capable of certifying a $0.1\%$ distortion tolerance in the former and $0.5\%$ in the latter, which is a significant achievement considering that these networks consist of multiple non-sparse layers. This study focuses on a specific subclass of topological graphs, namely those that can be drawn without edges crossing in a torus.  It has been previously established that a graph can be drawn on a torus if it has no divisions, equivalent to a connectivity value of less than three.  The main contribution of this research is to demonstrate that there is no upper limit to the size of a family of trees that can be drawn on a torus with no crossing edges, provided that the total number of vertices across all trees remains constant.  This finding establishes a clear distinction from planar graphs, in which there is an upper limit to the size of a family of graphs with a certain connectivity value.  It is also shown here that there is no equivalent result for spherical graphs, as certain families of trees with a constant number of vertices will always have a crossing number of at least one when drawn on a sphere.  An additional result of this research is the demonstration that the recognition problem for torus graphs is NP-complete, as is the recognition problem for a subcategory of torus graphs with no large odd cycles.  It is also shown here that there is no equivalent complex recognition result for the torus, as the recognition problem for torus graphs can be solved in O(n^2) time, making it more complex than planar graphs but less complex than trivial classes like series-parallel graphs. random walk on a graph is examined in this paper. Specifically, the pushawalk network, based on a given random walk on a $d$-dimensional torus, is analyzed. It has been shown that the pushawalk network is an arbitrary topological space for any random walk that is not stationary. However, when the random walk is stationary, its network exhibits topological characteristics equivalent to a series of disjoint circles. Additional findings related to random walks on graphs with group action are also presented, including the demonstration that certain networks are homeomorphic to tori or circles, depending on the specific properties of the associated random walk. Finally, distinguishability measures for binary random walks on graphs with two equal states are explored, leading to the discovery that equating two random walk spaces amounts to the same topological description as moving to the opposite side of a $d$-dimensional torus or placing an object on either side of a circle. Thus, topological considerations are found to be more refined indicators of binary random walk space equivalence than measure-based approaches. Furthermore, the study of pushawalk networks provides a novel perspective on binary random walk space equivalence, shifting the focus from specific graph characteristics to the topology of spaces defined by combined random walk data over time. Finally, numerous open questions remain in this field, including how general topological characteristics of a network might be from a given random walk, whether certain networks corresponding to mixing random walks are homeomorphic to a sphere, and how various binary random walk space equivalences that seem intuitively similar can differ topologically. Thus, this study also offers a range of possible research topics at the intersection of toplogy, probability theory, and computer science, related to binary random walk space equivalence and the topology of pushawalk networks.
